summary: Presents a framework for consent-based communications in SIP. SIP lets requests such as invitations and instant messages reach a recipient with no consent, which can be misused for abuse, including amplification and denial of service attacks. The framework lets a recipient grant permission before a relay sends them such requests. It was updated later.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP servers deliver messages to whoever the sender names, which makes them useful for spam and for denial-of-service attacks. This document says a server must first ask the person on the other end for permission, and must keep that permission only while it is wanted.

questions: how does sip prevent amplification attacks
what is a sip 470 consent needed response
subtitle: A framework that makes SIP servers ask recipients for permission before forwarding traffic to them.

tldr.problem: A network of SIP proxy servers delivers requests to recipients without asking them first. That lets an attacker make a server send messages to a large list of addresses, which is an amplification and denial-of-service attack.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC makes every relay obtain a permission from a recipient before it may forward traffic to it. The relay asks with a MESSAGE carrying a permission document, the recipient answers by publishing to a grant or deny URI, and the relay keeps a permission for each recipient it may talk to.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from October 2008 and was later updated by RFC 8217. It also adds a 470 Consent Needed response so a client learns which addresses still lack permission.

facts.label: How permission is granted
facts.value: SIP PUBLISH or HTTP GET to the grant URI

today: RFC 5360 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. It was later updated by RFC 8217; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: The Problem: Requests Without Consent
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol supports communications for several services, including real-time audio, video, text, instant messaging and presence. This communication is established by the transmission of various SIP requests, such as INVITE and MESSAGE, from an initiator to the recipient with whom communication is desired. Although a recipient can reject a request and decline the session, a network of SIP proxy servers will deliver a SIP request to its recipients without their explicit consent.

Receipt of these requests without explicit consent causes problems, including amplification and denial-of-service attacks, which are described in more detail in the companion requirements document RFC 4453. The RFC defines a basic framework for adding consent-based communication to SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Today a SIP server will happily forward a call or a message to anyone a stranger names. That makes it easy to turn a server into a spam machine, and to drown a network in traffic from one small request. This document changes that by requiring the server to ask first.

sections.title: Relays, Translations and the Consent Problem
sections.content:
Relays play a key role in this framework. A relay is any SIP server, be it a proxy, a Back-to-Back User Agent or some hybrid, that receives a request, translates its Request-URI into one or more next-hop URIs, and delivers the request to those URIs. The Request-URI of the incoming request is the target URI, and the destination URIs of the outgoing requests are the recipient URIs. The translation logic is the logic that defines a translation operation at a relay, including the translation's target and recipient URIs.

Through a translation operation, the relay can create outgoing requests to one or more additional recipient URIs, and that is what creates the consent problem. Two kinds of translation cause it. Translations based on local policy or local data, such as registrations, are the vehicle by which a request is delivered directly to an endpoint when it would not otherwise be possible. If a spammer has the address of a user, sip:user@example.com, it cannot deliver a MESSAGE request to the user agent of that user without access to the registration data that maps the address to the user agent. It is this use of registration data, and more generally the translation logic, that is expected to be authorized in order to prevent undesired communications. Translations that result in more than one recipient URI are a source of amplification: servers that do not perform translations, such as outbound proxy servers, do not cause amplification, while servers that do, such as inbound proxies authoritatively responsible for a SIP domain, may cause amplification if the user can be reached at multiple endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay takes one address in a request and turns it into one or more addresses to send to. That step is where consent is needed: the relay is the one that decides to deliver, so the relay is the one that must have permission.

sections.title: Permissions at a Relay
sections.content:
Relays implementing this framework obtain and store permissions associated with their translation logic. These permissions indicate whether or not a particular recipient has agreed to receive traffic at any given time, and recipients that have not given permission are simply ignored by the relay when it performs a translation. In principle, permissions are valid as long as the context in which they were granted is valid, or until they are revoked. For example, the permissions obtained by a URI-list SIP service that distributes MESSAGE requests to a set of recipients are valid as long as the service exists or until the permissions are revoked.

If a recipient is removed from a relay's translation logic, the relay SHOULD delete the permissions related to that recipient, for example when the registration of a contact URI expires. It is also RECOMMENDED that relays ask recipients to refresh their permissions periodically, and that a relay delete the permissions of a recipient that fails to refresh them for a given period of time. The RFC gives no guidance on the length of those intervals, because different applications have different requirements, and a relay dealing with recipients that do not implement this framework may want longer intervals since the refresh must then be performed by hand.

The framework aims to ensure that a relay only performs translations towards destinations that have given it permission. So when the translation logic is manipulated, for example when a new recipient URI is added, the relay obtains permission from the new recipient before installing the new logic. Relays ask for permission with MESSAGE requests. In the RFC's example, a relay hosting a URI-list service at sip:friends@example.com sends a MESSAGE request to sip:bob@example.org asking whether it may translate from the first address to the second. The request carries a permission document describing the translation and a human-readable part describing it as well, so that a user agent that does not understand permission documents can still show the request sensibly. The mechanism used to manipulate a relay's translation logic depends on the relay; the two existing mechanisms are the XML Configuration Access Protocol and REGISTER transactions.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay keeps a list of the recipients that agreed to hear from it, and it ignores anyone who did not. Permissions expire, so the relay is told to ask for them again from time to time and to drop the ones that are never refreshed.

sections.title: Adding a Recipient, Step by Step
sections.content:
Figure 4 of the RFC shows the complete process for adding a recipient URI to the translation logic of a relay. User A asks to add sip:B@example.com to the relay, step 1, using XCAP and the XML format for resource lists. Since the relay has no permission from that address, it places it in the pending state, as specified in RFC 5362. The relay answers with an HTTP 202 Accepted, step 2.

The relay then asks user B for permission, step 3, by sending a MESSAGE request carrying the permission document. Since user B is offline, the request is buffered by user B's store-and-forward server, which answers 202 Accepted in step 4. User A subscribes to the Pending Additions event package at the relay, step 5, to learn the outcome; the relay answers 200 OK and later sends a NOTIFY when the status changes. When user B comes online, the user agent fetches the stored messages, step 9, and they are delivered, step 10. User B authorizes the translation by publishing to the SIP URI to grant permissions contained in the document, step 11, and the relay answers 200 OK, step 12, and notifies user A, steps 13 and 14, that the permission has been received and the translation logic updated.

Two special cases are called out. When a request arrives carrying its own list of recipients, the relay checks whether it has permission for all the URIs in that list. If it does, it performs the translation. If it lacks permission for one or more URIs, it MUST NOT perform the translation and SHOULD return a 470 Consent Needed response with a Permission-Missing header field naming the URIs for which it has no permission. A client that receives a 470 without that header field has to use an alternative mechanism, such as XCAP, to discover which URIs were missing. Registrations are a different type of translation and deserve separate discussion, because a REGISTER transaction traditionally both sets up a translation and authorizes it. A third party can register a victim's contact URI under its own address of record, so the victim receives traffic that was addressed to the attacker; the framework therefore asks the registrar for permission in the same way, using a permission document that is typically general, asking for permission to forward any request from any sender to the recipient's URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding somebody to a mailing list now takes their agreement first. The server marks them as pending, asks them, and tells the person who made the request once the answer arrives. If the server meets a request it has no permission for, it refuses with a 470 and names the addresses that still need consent.

sections.title: Amplification Avoidance
sections.content:
Once a recipient is in the pending state, the relay needs to ask that recipient for permission by sending a MESSAGE request, and it must ensure that it is not used as an amplifier to launch amplification attacks. In such an attack the attacker adds a large number of recipient URIs to the translation logic of a relay, and the relay then sends a MESSAGE request to each of those recipients, so the bandwidth the relay generates is much higher than the bandwidth the attacker used to add those recipient URIs.

The framework uses a credit-based authorization mechanism to avoid this. It requires users adding new recipient URIs to a translation to generate an amount of bandwidth comparable to the bandwidth the relay will generate when sending MESSAGE requests towards those recipients. When XCAP is used, the requirement is met by not allowing clients to add more than one URI per HTTP transaction. When a REGISTER transaction is used, it is met by not allowing clients to register more than one contact per REGISTER transaction. Relays implementing this framework MUST NOT allow clients to add more than one recipient URI per transaction. If a client using XCAP tries to add more than one recipient URI in a single HTTP transaction, the XCAP server SHOULD return an HTTP 409 Conflict response and describe the reason in an XML body using the constraint-failure element. If a client tries to register more than one contact in a single REGISTER transaction, the registrar SHOULD return a SIP 403 response and explain the refusal in its reason phrase.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking a server to send to many people at once is the attack this framework has to stop. So the rule is simple: one address per request from the client, which costs the attacker about as much bandwidth as the server will spend.

sections.title: What a Permission Document Contains
sections.content:
A permission document is the representation, for example encoded in XML, of a permission. It contains the identity of the sender for whom permissions are granted, the identity of the original recipient, which is the input to the translation operation and is also called the target URI, and the identity of the final recipient, which is the result of the translation and is also called the recipient URI. It also contains URIs to grant permission, which recipients can use to allow the relay to perform the translation described in the document, and URIs to deny permission, which they can use to refuse it. Relays MUST support the use of SIP and SIPS URIs in permission documents and MAY support HTTP and HTTPS URIs.

Permission documents can contain wildcards. A document can request permission for any relay to forward requests coming from a particular sender to a particular recipient, in which case the field holding the identity of the original recipient matches any URI. However, the recipient URI MUST NOT be wildcarded. Entities implementing the framework MUST support the permission document format defined in RFC 5361 and MAY support other formats. In the RFC's example, the document sent by the relay says: any sender; original recipient sip:friends@example.com; final recipient sip:B@example.com; a SIP URI and an HTTPS URI to grant permission; and a SIP URI and an HTTPS URI to deny permission. The Sender field is expected often to contain a wildcard, but scenarios involving request-contained URI lists can require documents that apply to a specific sender, and in cases where the identity of the sender matters, relays MUST authenticate senders.
sections.plainLanguage: The document states which address is asking, which address the traffic is meant for, which address will actually receive it, and the two links the recipient can use to say yes or no. The recipient address can never be a wildcard.

sections.title: Granting, Denying and Proving Identity
sections.content:
A recipient gives a relay permission by sending a SIP PUBLISH or an HTTP GET request to one of the URIs to grant permissions in the document, and denies permission by using one of the URIs to deny permissions. Requests to grant or deny permissions contain an empty body. When a recipient wants to revoke a permission it uses the URI it received in the document to deny the permission it previously granted. If the recipient loses that URI, it must wait until it receives a new request produced by the translation, which carries a Trigger-Consent header field with a URI and a target-uri header field parameter identifying the target URI of the translation; the recipient sends a PUBLISH request with an empty body to that URI to receive a fresh MESSAGE request with a permission document that carries a new URI to revoke with.

Relays MUST ensure that the PUBLISH or HTTP GET request came from the recipient of the translation and not from an attacker, and they have four methods to do so. With SIP identity, the relay MUST check that the originator of the PUBLISH is the owner of the recipient URI in the document, and otherwise SHOULD answer 401 Unauthorized and MUST NOT process the request further. P-Asserted-Identity works the same way, but the RFC notes that this mechanism is intended for use only within networks of trusted SIP servers, inside an administrative domain with previously agreed policies. A return routability test provides less security than SIP identity but is better than nothing where SIP identity is not available, which the RFC calls the current Internet: the relay generates an unguessable URI with a cryptographically random user part and puts it in the permission document, and any incoming request to that URI SHOULD be considered authenticated. It is the only method that allows HTTP URIs in permission documents. Relays using a return routability test MUST send the MESSAGE request with the permission document to a SIPS URI, so that attackers do not get access to the unguessable URI, and the document MUST contain only secure URIs, with a part of each, such as the user part of a SIPS URI, cryptographically random with at least 32 bits of randomness. SIP digest can authenticate the sender of a PUBLISH request as long as that sender shares a secret with the relay, for example a recipient in the same domain as the relay.
sections.plainLanguage: To say yes or no, the recipient contacts a link in the permission document. The server has to be sure that the person replying is the person being contacted, so it can check the SIP identity, a trusted-network identity header, a shared secret, or simply require the reply to come back to an unguessable address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Relays generally implement security mechanisms for client authentication and authorization, and clients are typically authenticated before they can manipulate a relay's translation logic. Those mechanisms fall out of the scope of this framework, but even with them in place relays still need this framework, because authentication of a client does not stop an authorized client from adding recipients to a translation without their consent. Relays performing translations MUST therefore implement this framework.

When return routability tests are used, the URIs used to grant or deny permissions need to be protected from attackers, and SIPS URIs provide a good tool for that. Where store-and-forward servers are used, the interface between a user agent and its store-and-forward server is frequently not based on SIP, so SIPS cannot secure those URIs; implementations of store-and-forward servers MUST provide a mechanism for delivering encrypted and integrity-protected messages to their user agents. The information provided by the Pending Additions event package can be sensitive, so relays need strong means for authentication and information confidentiality, and SIPS URIs are a good mechanism for that.

Permission documents can reveal sensitive information, and attackers may try to modify them so that clients grant or deny permissions different from the ones they think they are granting. It is RECOMMENDED that relays use strong means for integrity protection and confidentiality when sending permission documents to clients. The mechanism used for conveying information to clients SHOULD ensure integrity and confidentiality, and an end-to-end SIP encryption mechanism such as S/MIME SHOULD be used to achieve it. If strong end-to-end security is not available, hop-by-hop security based on TLS and SIPS URIs is RECOMMENDED instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Authenticating the person who asks for a change is not the same as protecting the people who will receive it. The permission document and the answers to it carry private information, so they should be encrypted, and the store-and-forward server that holds them must deliver them intact.

viz.caption: THE PROTOTYPICAL CALL FLOW FROM RFC 5360

messages.label: ADD RECIPIENT
messages.note: The client asks the relay to add a recipient URI.

messages.label: 202 ACCEPTED
messages.note: The relay puts the new recipient in the pending state.

messages.label: MESSAGE WITH PERMISSION DOCUMENT
messages.note: The relay asks the recipient for permission, with URIs to grant or deny.

messages.label: REQUEST FOR STORED MESSAGES
messages.note: The recipient comes online and collects what was buffered.

messages.label: PUBLISH TO THE GRANT URI
messages.note: The recipient grants permission by publishing to one of the URIs in the document.

messages.label: NOTIFY
messages.note: The relay tells the client that the permission was granted and the translation installed.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TO PROVE THE GRANT OR DENY CAME FROM THE RECIPIENT

items.title: SIP identity
items.text: The relay checks that the originator of the request owns the recipient URI.

items.title: P-Asserted-Identity
items.text: A trusted-network header, usable only inside an administrative domain with agreed policies.

items.title: Return routability
items.text: The reply must reach an unguessable address with at least 32 bits of randomness.

items.title: SIP digest
items.text: Works when the recipient shares a secret with the relay, such as in the same domain.
